Trying to Conceive

Follitropin alfa injections: use, handling and monitoring

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Follitropin alfa supplies FSH as part of a specialist fertility plan. Knowing the purpose of each injection, how to handle your exact product and when to contact the clinic can make a complicated schedule easier to follow.

What follitropin alfa is

Follitropin alfa is a manufactured form of follicle-stimulating hormone, usually shortened to FSH. The body normally makes FSH in the pituitary gland. In the ovaries it supports the growth of follicles, the small structures containing eggs; in the testes it helps support sperm production.

The medicine is made using recombinant DNA technology and is available under brand names including GONAL-f. Names, licensed uses and available presentations vary between countries. It may come as powder with a supplied solvent, a multidose preparation or a prefilled pen. These products are not interchangeable simply because the active ingredient sounds familiar.

Why it may be prescribed for ovarian treatment

A fertility specialist may prescribe follitropin alfa to support ovulation when it is not occurring reliably, sometimes after an oral treatment such as clomiphene has not worked. In severe FSH and LH deficiency, an LH-containing medicine may also be needed. The appropriate first treatment depends on the diagnosis and local guidance.

For IVF or another assisted-reproduction cycle, the aim may be to develop several follicles so eggs can be collected. This differs from trying to produce a limited response for ovulation induction. Follitropin alfa cannot correct every cause of infertility and is not effective treatment for primary ovarian failure. Follicle growth does not guarantee a pregnancy or a live birth.

Use in selected male hormone deficiencies

Follitropin alfa can also be used for selected people with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, where inadequate hormonal stimulation contributes to low or absent sperm production. It is used with human chorionic gonadotrophin, or hCG, and is not a general remedy for every low sperm count.

In the US GONAL-f regimen, hCG is used first to bring testosterone into the intended range, then continued when FSH treatment is added. Response takes time and is assessed with hormone measurements and semen testing. Primary testicular failure is a different problem and is not corrected by simply increasing the stimulation. A male treatment schedule must never be copied into an ovarian-stimulation plan.

Dose and monitoring are part of one plan

The dose, start date and duration depend on the treatment goal, previous response, ovarian reserve or hormone findings and other individual factors. The prescription may change during a cycle. Use the latest written instructions rather than an old message or another patient’s schedule.

During ovarian stimulation, ultrasound and, when needed, blood tests guide the next step. The clinic may adjust the dose, change the trigger plan or cancel a cycle if the response is unsafe. A stronger response is not always better. Keep monitoring appointments even when you feel well, and do not increase or reduce the dose independently.

Learn the technique for the product you receive

The GONAL-f presentations discussed here are injected under the skin. An intramuscular injection is not an interchangeable option. Have a nurse or pharmacist demonstrate the exact pen or vial, how to measure the prescribed dose and what to do if you are unsure how much was delivered.

If mixing is required, use the specified solvent and instructions. Check that the prepared solution has the expected appearance; do not use it if it is unexpectedly cloudy, discoloured or contains particles. Use clean technique, change injection sites as taught and place used needles in an appropriate sharps container.

Do not share a pen or reuse needles. If you miss a dose, make a dosing error or cannot complete an injection, contact the fertility service for instructions. Do not double the next dose or guess how much extra to inject.

Storage rules differ between vials and pens

Check the leaflet supplied with your own medicine before storing, mixing or travelling with it. “Keep every form refrigerated” and “use every mixed vial immediately” are not rules that apply to every presentation. Record the opening or mixing date and any discard date the pharmacist gives you.

For example, the European single-use 75 IU powder presentation is stored at no more than 25°C, protected from light, and used immediately after reconstitution. European prefilled pens have different unopened-storage instructions; after opening, the cited information permits storage between 2°C and 25°C for up to 28 days. Do not freeze the pens.

The US multidose product also has a 28-day limit after mixing under its specified conditions. This does not allow leftover medicine from a single-use vial to be kept for 28 days. If a product was frozen, overheated or left out beyond its permitted time, ask the pharmacist before using it. These examples do not replace the label for your country and pack.

Conditions that may make treatment unsuitable

Before treatment, the specialist checks for reasons the medicine should not be used. These include a serious reaction to recombinant FSH or an ingredient, primary ovarian or testicular failure, and certain uncontrolled endocrine disorders. Thyroid or adrenal problems may need appropriate treatment first.

Relevant pituitary or hypothalamic tumours, hormone-dependent cancers involving reproductive organs or the breast, unexplained uterine bleeding, or an ovarian cyst or enlargement of uncertain origin also need assessment. A label’s reference to unexplained ovarian enlargement is not the same as saying everyone with the syndrome formerly called PCOS is excluded.

Tell the clinic if pregnancy is possible or you are breastfeeding. Follitropin alfa is not intended for use during pregnancy, and the cited GONAL-f information advises against use while breastfeeding. If pregnancy is discovered or an accidental exposure occurs, contact the team for individual advice; do not assume the exposure proves harm.

Share your medical history and all other treatments

Mention previous blood clots, stroke, heart disease, chest pain conditions, asthma or other lung disease, ovarian cysts and earlier reactions to fertility medicines. These details help the team assess risk and plan monitoring; they do not all mean that treatment is automatically impossible.

Give the team a list of prescription medicines, pharmacy products, vitamins, herbal remedies and other hormones. Other fertility medicines can alter the ovarian response and the dose needed. Do not add clomiphene, hCG, LH or another fertility product yourself, and do not mix products in one syringe unless specifically instructed for those products.

Which symptoms can be less serious?

Injection-site soreness, redness or bruising, headache, nausea, mild abdominal discomfort or bloating can occur. Breast tenderness, tiredness and mood changes may also occur during fertility treatment, which often involves more than one medicine. In male treatment, acne and breast enlargement have been reported.

Symptoms such as heartburn, appetite change, diarrhoea, anxiety, reduced sexual interest or erection difficulties should be discussed if they are new or troublesome. They are not all established common effects of follitropin alfa itself; the underlying condition, other medicines and stress can contribute. Unexpected vaginal bleeding also deserves advice.

Do not let a long side-effect list make every symptom seem harmless. Mild discomfort and a serious complication can overlap at first. Report worsening symptoms, and use the urgent contact plan rather than waiting for a routine appointment if pain, swelling or vomiting increases.

Recognising ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, or OHSS, is an excessive response to stimulation. The ovaries can enlarge and fluid can move out of blood vessels into the abdomen and, in severe cases, other spaces. The problem is more than simply having a large number of follicles.

Contact the fertility team urgently for increasing abdominal pain or swelling, rapid weight gain, persistent vomiting, marked thirst or passing much less urine. Breathing difficulty, chest pain or collapse needs emergency care. Do not take another scheduled injection or trigger without urgent advice if a serious reaction is suspected.

OHSS can develop or worsen after the final stimulation injection, especially if pregnancy occurs. Keep follow-up appointments and the clinic’s emergency number available. Do not try to manage substantial symptoms only by changing how much you drink or by waiting for the hormones to wear off.

Other symptoms that need emergency assessment

Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain, often with nausea, may indicate ovarian torsion, where the ovary twists. A painful, warm or swollen leg, sudden breathlessness or chest pain can indicate a blood clot. These need urgent assessment, not reassurance based on the fact that you are taking fertility medicine.

Call emergency services for signs of a severe allergic reaction, such as tongue or throat swelling, wheezing or collapse. Sudden speech or vision problems, loss of balance, weakness or confusion may be stroke symptoms. Chest discomfort spreading to the jaw or arm, especially with sweating, breathlessness or faintness, also needs emergency care.

A positive pregnancy test does not end all monitoring. Pain or bleeding in early pregnancy may require assessment for an ectopic pregnancy. Tell the service about your fertility treatment and whether an ultrasound has confirmed the pregnancy’s location.

The trigger and multiple-pregnancy plan

FSH helps follicles grow; a trigger medicine is a separate part of some treatment protocols. Depending on the plan, the trigger may contain hCG or another medicine. Its exact timing is important, and it may be withheld or changed when the response is excessive.

Developing several follicles can raise the chance of twins or a higher-order pregnancy in ovulation-induction treatment. In IVF, the embryo-transfer plan is another major influence. Ask how the clinic limits this risk and whether you should avoid unprotected sex if a cycle is cancelled or the ovaries are enlarged. Do not improvise a trigger because the scan appears encouraging.

Making the treatment manageable

Ask for a schedule that lists the medicine, dose, time, monitoring appointments and who to call outside office hours. Keep it updated when the plan changes. If you or a partner give injections, practise the technique with the clinical team until the steps are clear.

Discuss smoking and alcohol with the fertility team; stopping smoking and avoiding alcohol when pregnancy may occur support preconception health. They are not a promise to multiply the medicine’s success. If treatment affects sleep, mood, work or intimacy, ask for practical and emotional support as well as medication advice.

Correct storage, technique and monitoring reduce avoidable problems but cannot eliminate every risk. The aim is a response that is appropriate and safe for your situation, with a clear next step whether the cycle proceeds, changes or stops.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The treatment indication and monitored response determine the schedule.

Storage, mixing and injection instructions belong to the exact product supplied.

How BeMama can help

Keep one current written schedule and an after-hours contact number with your medicine.

When to seek help

Increasing abdominal pain or swelling, rapid weight gain, persistent vomiting or reduced urine needs urgent fertility-team advice. Severe breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, neurological symptoms or a severe allergic reaction needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • FSH treatment supports selected ovarian or sperm-production problems.
  • Do not change a dose or trigger without the clinic’s instructions.
  • A 28-day rule does not apply to every vial or pen.
  • OHSS can appear after stimulation injections stop.
  • Monitoring supports safer care but does not guarantee pregnancy.

Frequently asked questions

Is follitropin alfa the same hormone the body makes?

It is a manufactured form of FSH, produced using recombinant DNA technology. It acts on the reproductive system, but a prescribed treatment schedule is different from normal hormone production.

Is it prescribed only for IVF?

No. It can be used for selected ovulation problems and, with other hormones, some forms of male hypogonadism. These indications use different schedules and monitoring.

Should I increase the dose if the response seems slow?

No. The clinic considers scans, hormone results and the full treatment plan. Increasing it yourself can create risk without solving the reason for a limited response.

Can I inject it into a muscle instead of under the skin?

Not for the GONAL-f presentations described here. Use the route and technique taught for your exact product. Do not treat routes as interchangeable.

Can every mixed vial be kept for 28 days?

No. Some single-use products must be used immediately after mixing; specific multidose products and pens have different limits. Follow the supplied leaflet and pharmacist’s instructions.

What should I do if I miss a dose or make an injection error?

Contact the fertility clinic for product- and timing-specific advice. Do not double a dose or guess an additional amount.

Can OHSS start after the injections have stopped?

Yes, and pregnancy can make it persist or worsen. Report increasing swelling, pain, vomiting or reduced urine promptly; breathing problems or collapse require emergency care.

Does abdominal bloating always mean OHSS?

No. Mild discomfort can occur during stimulation, but symptoms can overlap. Increasing pain, swelling, rapid weight gain or illness needs assessment rather than a home diagnosis.

Is the trigger always hCG?

No. The trigger and timing depend on the protocol and response. The team may use another medicine, change the plan or withhold the trigger if the response is unsafe.

Will correct technique guarantee a pregnancy?

No. It helps avoid preventable dosing and handling problems, but success also depends on the diagnosis and many other factors. Ask what outcome each treatment stage is intended to achieve.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
